title: Environment & Secrets
subtitle: Storing API keys safely, deployment environments, and required reviewers

content.text: Secrets — never put API keys in code

Secrets are encrypted values stored in GitHub (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions). They're injected as environment variables in workflows and masked in logs — if a secret value accidentally appears in output, GitHub replaces it with ***. They are never visible after being saved.

content.code:
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Secrets are accessed via the secrets context
      - name: Deploy to server
        env:
          SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}
          SERVER_HOST: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
        run: |
          echo "$SSH_KEY" > /tmp/key && chmod 600 /tmp/key
          ssh -i /tmp/key deploy@$SERVER_HOST 'cd /app && docker compose pull && docker compose up -d'

      # Many actions accept secrets directly in 'with:'
      - name: Push to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # GITHUB_TOKEN is a special auto-generated token — no setup needed
      # Has write access to the repo, packages, and PRs
      - name: Create GitHub Release
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          files: dist/*
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

# Workflow-level env (available to all jobs and steps)
env:
  NODE_ENV: production
  API_URL: https://api.myapp.com

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    # Job-level env (overrides workflow-level for this job)
    env:
      DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.PROD_DATABASE_URL }}

    steps:
      - name: Build
        # Step-level env (highest priority, only for this step)
        env:
          BUILD_TARGET: production
        run: npm run build:$BUILD_TARGET

      # vars context: non-secret config variables (set in repo settings)
      # Use for non-sensitive config that varies per environment
      - name: Deploy
        run: echo "Deploying to ${{ vars.DEPLOY_REGION }}"

# In GitHub: Settings → Environments → New environment
# Configure: required reviewers, deployment branches, environment secrets

jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging   # uses 'staging' environment (auto-created)
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying to staging..."

  deploy-production:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: deploy-staging
    # 'production' environment can have required reviewers:
    # → deploy-production won't proceed until a reviewer approves
    environment: production
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying to production..."

# With environment-specific secrets:
# Staging environment has: DEPLOY_HOST=staging.myapp.com
# Production environment has: DEPLOY_HOST=myapp.com
# The right secret is automatically used based on the environment: field
jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}  # from workflow_dispatch input
    steps:
      - run: ssh deploy@${{ secrets.DEPLOY_HOST }} './deploy.sh'

content.text: Use environment-specific secrets for staging vs production. Create a 'staging' environment and a 'production' environment in GitHub. Give each the same secret names but different values (e.g. DEPLOY_HOST). The right values are automatically injected based on the environment: field in your job — no if-conditions needed.

questions.question: A developer accidentally adds 'echo ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}' to a workflow step. What happens when the workflow runs?
options: The workflow fails with a permissions error
GitHub masks the secret value in the logs, replacing it with ***
The secret value is visible in the workflow logs
GitHub refuses to run the workflow and alerts the team
questions.explanation: GitHub automatically scans all workflow output for secret values and replaces them with *** in the logs. This prevents accidental exposure. However, this is a safety net — you should never intentionally output secrets. Some techniques (base64 encoding, escaping) can sometimes bypass masking, so treat it as defense-in-depth, not primary protection.

faq.q: What is the difference between secrets and vars?
faq.a: 'secrets' are encrypted and masked in logs — use for API keys, passwords, tokens. 'vars' (variables) are stored in plain text and visible in logs — use for non-sensitive config like region names, image registries, feature flags. Both can be set at repo level, environment level, or organization level.

examples: Required reviewers on a production environment means no code reaches prod without a senior engineer approving — GitHub Actions enforces this automatically
GITHUB_TOKEN is used by millions of workflows to push to npm, create releases, comment on PRs, and deploy to GitHub Pages — all without any secret setup
